drills.q: Explain composition over configuration with a concrete example of where a prop-driven API breaks down, and whether composition is strictly better.
drills.a: A prop-driven Card (imageUrl, title, footerButtons, showDivider...) accumulates a prop per new requirement and eventually can't express an unanticipated layout. A composed API (<Card><Card.Image/></Card>) lets consumers arrange primitives directly. Not strictly better -- composition costs more consumer code for genuinely uniform, simple components where a well-configured prop API with defaults is faster and harder to misuse.

drills.q: How does a compound component share state between its parts without prop drilling, and what does the consumer still control?
drills.a: A parent component holds shared state and provides it via React Context scoped to the compound component; children consume it internally instead of the consumer manually wiring props between them. The consumer still fully controls DOM arrangement and structure, which a monolithic prop API couldn't offer.

drills.q: What problem does the W3C DTCG token standard solve, and what mechanism lets a semantic token reference a primitive one?
drills.a: Before a shared standard (first stable spec Oct 2025), every design tool/pipeline used its own token format, causing manual, error-prone, drift-prone translation between Figma, build pipelines, and code. Token aliasing (e.g. {color.blue.500} inside a semantic token's $value) lets a semantic token point at a primitive, which is the mechanism theming depends on -- components reference only the semantic layer.

drills.q: A component looks fine in light mode but has unreadable low-contrast text in dark mode. Diagnose the architectural cause and a systemic prevention.
drills.a: The component almost certainly references a primitive token directly (hardcoded gray-900) instead of a semantic token (color-text-primary) meant to resolve differently per theme, bypassing the indirection layer. Prevent systemically with a lint rule/token-usage linter in CI that flags direct primitive-token references in component code.

drills.q: Why is versioning a design system genuinely harder than a typical utility library, using a concrete example?
drills.a: Semver assumes the public surface equals the code API, but a token change (e.g. a 2px spacing adjustment) can silently break visual layout across dozens of surfaces with zero function-signature change -- looking like a safe patch while behaving like a breaking change. A mature team runs visual regression across the whole system and treats token renames with API-breaking-change rigor, not routine patch releases.

drills.q: When is building a formal design system premature, and what should happen instead if a second product is planned for 'sometime next year'?
drills.a: Premature for a single product/team with no concrete near-term second consumer -- coordination overhead (versioned package, cross-team review, deprecation policy) only pays off with genuine reuse. For a vaguely planned future second product, avoid building the formal system now (risks guessed requirements); document existing shared patterns lightly and do the formal extraction once the second product's real needs are known.

drills.q: Compare headless/behavior-only component libraries vs fully styled opinionated ones, and state which fits a product needing strong brand differentiation.
drills.a: Headless (Radix, React Aria): correct ARIA/keyboard logic solved once, zero visual opinion, more setup per team. Fully styled (Material UI, Chakra): fastest to consistent UI, but fights distinctive differentiation since consistency IS its value proposition. A product needing strong brand differentiation should choose headless, since fully opinionated systems impose a default look that works against differentiation.

drills.q: A design system's Button has an open style prop most teams use regularly to override appearance. What does this indicate and how do you address it, and is adding more variants always the fix?
drills.a: It indicates the variant system hasn't captured the real design space -- the system provides an illusion of consistency silently bypassed in practice, arguably worse than visible inconsistency since it's often not caught in review. Address by auditing actual override usage and formalizing recurring patterns as first-class variants. Not always the fix: if usage is highly varied/product-specific rather than converging on recurring patterns, the better fix may be a genuine composition point (slot, render prop) rather than an ever-growing incomplete variant list.

drills.q: What happens if a consumer renders a compound subcomponent (e.g. Tabs.Tab) outside its provider, and how should a well-designed API handle it?
drills.a: The context value is null/undefined. A well-designed compound component should explicitly guard this and throw a clear developer-facing error (e.g. "Tabs.Tab must be used within a Tabs component") rather than silently failing or throwing an obscure runtime error from destructuring null.

drills.q: A designer changes a spacing token by 2px and engineering ships it as a routine patch release. What's the actual risk, and how should a mature team handle it differently?
drills.a: The risk is silent layout breakage across every surface referencing that token, shipped with no one specifically reviewing the blast radius since it looks trivial. A mature team runs visual regression across the whole system before releasing any token change and treats token value changes/renames with deliberate versioning rigor comparable to an API change, not a routine patch.
